question: Tell me about a time when you went above and beyond for a customer. Why did you do it? How did the customer respond? What was the outcome?

raiseTranscript.text: A customer reported that our checkout flow was dropping their orders on mobile. I stayed late to reproduce it on three devices, found a CSS overflow bug, and pushed a hotfix the same night after getting quick review from my mentor.
Why did you take it on yourself instead of handing it to on-call?
The ticket was assigned to me and the customer had already waited two days. I didn't want to lose their trust.
They emailed back saying the fix worked and they completed their purchase. They also left a positive review.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Fixed mobile checkout bug same day after reproducing on multiple devices
Quote: "I didn't want to lose their trust"
Outcome: customer completed purchase and left positive review
Follow-up: Why take it yourself? -> Owned because ticket was assigned to me and prior delay
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Customer Obsession for a junior. The candidate took personal ownership of a customer-impacting bug instead of routing it elsewhere. They reproduced the issue across devices and shipped a fix the same evening after securing a quick review. The customer completed their purchase and left positive feedback, directly tying the extra effort to a concrete result. This shows appropriate individual scope and willingness to go beyond assigned hours. The main strength is clear ownership of their own work with visible customer outcome.

lowerTranscript.text: A customer asked for a feature we didn't have. I told them we'd consider it for the roadmap and closed the ticket.
Not really, it was outside my team's current sprint.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Response: told them it would be considered for roadmap and closed ticket
Follow-up: Did you do anything else? -> No, outside current sprint
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Customer Obsession for a junior. The candidate treated the request as a standard ticket closure without exploring any workaround or escalation. No attempt was made to understand the customer's need or protect their experience. The follow-up confirmed the decision was driven by sprint boundaries rather than customer impact. This reflects minimal ownership even at the individual contributor level.

raiseTranscript.text: An enterprise customer was hitting rate limits that blocked their integration. I worked with the platform team to temporarily raise their limits and then drove a change to make limits configurable per tier.
The customer renewed and expanded their contract. The change also reduced similar tickets by 40% across the board.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Enterprise customer blocked by rate limits
Coordinated with platform team for temp raise then made limits configurable
Quote: "The customer renewed and expanded their contract"
Outcome: 40% reduction in similar tickets
Follow-up: What drove the permanent change? -> Cross-team influence to prevent recurrence
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Customer Obsession for a senior. The candidate did not stop at a temporary workaround and instead influenced another team to make limits configurable. This produced both a renewed contract and a 40% drop in related tickets. The story shows cross-team impact and a focus on systemic customer pain rather than one-off heroics. The biggest strength is turning a single customer issue into a durable product improvement.

lowerTranscript.text: A customer complained about slow responses. I forwarded the ticket to support and checked in a week later.
I assume so, but I didn't follow up further.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Forwarded to support and checked in once
Follow-up: Did response time improve? -> Assumed yes without further follow-up
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Customer Obsession for a senior. The candidate delegated the issue and performed only a single check-in without verifying resolution or looking for patterns. No attempt was made to influence process changes or reduce future occurrences. This shows limited ownership and no cross-team leverage despite the level.

raiseTranscript.text: Our team was consistently missing SLAs for a key customer segment. I ran a retro with the team, identified root causes, and created a rotation where senior engineers paired with support on high-severity tickets.
NPS for that segment rose 18 points and the team reported higher confidence handling escalations.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Team missing SLAs for key segment
Ran retro, created engineer-support rotation
Outcome: NPS up 18 points and team confidence improved
Follow-up: What changed for the team? -> Built process that raised both customer and team metrics
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Customer Obsession for a manager. The candidate diagnosed a team-level SLA problem and introduced a new operating rhythm that improved both customer NPS and internal capability. The 18-point NPS lift and reported team confidence demonstrate leverage through the team rather than personal heroics. The story shows clear ownership of team outcomes tied directly to customer results.

lowerTranscript.text: A customer was unhappy with delivery delays. I asked the team to prioritize their requests going forward.
Did you change any team processes?
Not formally, just reminded them in standup.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Asked team to prioritize the customer's requests
Follow-up: Any process change? -> Informal reminder only
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Customer Obsession for a manager. The candidate issued a one-time instruction without creating any lasting team mechanism or tracking impact. No evidence of coaching or systemic improvement was shown. This reflects weak leverage and limited ownership of team-level customer outcomes.

raiseTranscript.text: Customer research showed our pricing was creating friction for mid-market segments and risking long-term growth. I led a pricing restructure that traded short-term revenue for broader adoption, despite internal pushback.
Mid-market revenue grew 3x in 18 months and churn dropped 12%. We also used the same customer insight process for two subsequent product bets.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Pricing friction blocking mid-market growth
Led pricing restructure trading short-term revenue for adoption
Outcome: 3x mid-market revenue, 12% churn drop
Follow-up: How did you handle internal resistance? -> Used customer data to drive strategic trade-off
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Customer Obsession for an exec. The candidate used customer insight to drive a strategic pricing change that accepted short-term revenue pressure for long-term market position. The 3x revenue growth and 12% churn reduction show org-level impact. The approach also scaled into a repeatable process for future decisions. The core strength is strategic judgment grounded in customer data over internal comfort.

lowerTranscript.text: We received feedback that customers wanted more integrations. I asked product to add it to the roadmap.
Did you personally engage with customers or change investment?
I reviewed the quarterly roadmap updates.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer
Asked product to add to roadmap
Follow-up: Personal engagement or investment change? -> Only reviewed roadmap updates
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Customer Obsession for an exec. The candidate delegated the request and performed only passive oversight without reallocating resources or engaging directly. No strategic trade-off or long-term thinking was demonstrated. This shows insufficient leverage at the organizational level.

diagnostic.exec: Scaled insight process to future bets
